newsitem.title: UK: British government loses votes in upper house.
newsitem.headline: British government loses votes in upper house.

text.p: Britain's ruling Conservatives, teetering on a knife-edge with no majority in Parliament, lost a vote on Monday night in the upper House of Lords.

The vote, which does not threaten Prime Minister John Major's hold on power, concerned the government's plan to give the police strong powers to counter organised crime by bugging suspects without the prior approval of a judge.

Members of the Lords voted 206 to 145 to support a proposal by the opposition Labour Party to force police to get permission from special watchdog commissioners before bugging anyone, except in emergencies.

Just a few minutes later the government lost another vote when the Lords backed an amendment offered by the opposition Liberal Democrats requiring circuit judges, not watchdog commissioners, to authorise bugging operations.
Members of the unelected house shouted "resign" as the vote was announced.
Labour had once backed the bill but changed its stance after criticism from civil liberties campaigners, judges and senior Labour politicians.
It was another blow for Home Secretary (interior minister) Michael Howard, who had tried to face down a deluge of criticism over the bugging idea.

Howard, who has responsibility for police and prisons, has been embarrassed in the past year by a string of adverse court rulings and by critical inquiries into break-outs from two top high-security prisons.
"The government attaches the greatest importance to ensuring that the police can continue to use these valuable techniques, on a statutory basis," the Home Office said.
"It will now be considering carefully the position in the light of the amendments and will respond in due course."
The government may try to overturn the defeat when the bill returns to the lower house of Commons. The House of Lords has the power to amend bills but does not make law.
Major must call a national election by May 22, unless his party loses a vote of confidence in the Commons before then.
